audio.t: Good afternoon, everyone. I'm Doctor Chen from the Office of Academic Affairs, and today I want to talk about academic integrity, especially now that midterm papers are due. Many students think plagiarism only means copying a whole essay. In fact, it also includes using someone else's ideas without giving credit, buying assignments online, and submitting the same paper to two different courses without permission.

This semester, the university has also updated its policy on A I tools. You may use them to brainstorm or check your grammar, but only if your instructor allows it, and you must state clearly how you used them. Copying text from a chatbot and presenting it as your own work is treated the same way as copying from a book.

So what happens if a case is reported? For a first offense, you will usually receive a zero on the assignment and must complete an online integrity course. A second offense may lead to failing the course. If you are unsure about any rule, please visit the Writing Center before you submit, not after.

questions.explain: 講者開場即說要談 academic integrity，並說明抄襲範圍、AI 規定與違規後果。期中只是背景；AI 只在教師允許下可用，並非鼓勵使用。
options: To explain academic integrity rules and the consequences of breaking them

head: From: Amy Hsu (TA, Introduction to Sociology)
To: SOC101 students
Subject: Midterm paper submission and similarity reports
passage: Hi everyone, this is a reminder that your midterm paper is due on Friday, November 6, at 11:59 p.m. Please upload it to the course page on the learning platform as a Word or PDF file. Papers sent by email will not be accepted.

After you upload your file, the system will automatically generate a similarity report. Don't panic if your score is not zero. Quotations, references, and common phrases are often highlighted. Professor Huang will manually review any report above 25 percent to decide whether there is a real problem.

You may submit as many times as you like before the deadline, and only the final version will be graded. If you would like feedback on your citations, I will hold extra office hours on Wednesday afternoon in Room 412. Best, Amy

passage: A recent survey by the Student Association has found that many students at the university are confused about the rules of academic integrity. Of the 1,200 undergraduates who responded, nearly 40 percent said they were not sure whether using an AI tool to rewrite a paragraph counts as plagiarism, and almost a third admitted they had never read the university's integrity guidelines.

The results did not surprise Professor Lisa Wu, who chairs the Academic Integrity Committee. "Most cases we see are not about students trying to cheat," she said. "They are about students who don't know how to paraphrase or cite properly, especially when they are writing in English for the first time." She noted that the number of reported cases rose last year, mainly in courses taught in English.

To address the problem, the committee will launch two programs next semester. First, all first-year students will be required to complete a two-hour online module on citation and paraphrasing before they can register for second-semester courses. Second, the Writing Center will train twenty senior students as "integrity mentors" who can answer questions in Mandarin or English during evening hours.

Not everyone is convinced. Some students worry that the new module will simply become another box to check. "A video and a quiz won't teach me how to write," said Jason Lee, a sophomore in engineering. "What I need is feedback on my actual assignments." Professor Wu responded that instructors will also be encouraged to include short citation exercises in their courses.
